newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian premier says EU wave expansion wrong.
newsitem.headline: Romanian premier says EU wave expansion wrong.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said on Wednesday the European Union was wrong to proceed with expansion in waves and pledged to foster reforms to reverse a decision to deny his country early entry.

Ciorbea said the EU Commission's decision to start membership talks only with Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia was not comparable to NATO's move last week to limit eastward expansion to three countries.
"Expansion by waves is justified in the case of NATO, but it is not justified for European Union enlargement, which is a process of continuous integration," he told a news conference.
"We will continue our political and diplomatic fight right through until December for the adoption of a political decision on EU expansion."

The EU decision unveiled in Strasbourg left Romania and four other countries on the sidelines for talks -- Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia and Bulgaria. A final ruling will be announced at an EU summit in December in Luxembourg.

An EU assessment of Romania said the Balkan country had made considerable progress since launching political and economic reforms under a new centrist government but that these had not yet translated into economic growth.

Ciorbea said his administration would press on with the reform programme, backed by international lenders, "to prepare for NATO membership in 1999 and for EU admission...when we have fulfilled all criteria, especially economic ones.
"Above all, when we are able to compete, when our commercial companies can stand real competition from big European holdings."
Romania's centrist government had concentrated efforts on winning early entry to NATO on the assumption that it met alliance membership criteria more easily.

The country's leaders gracefully accepted NATO's decision to take in Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic in the "first wave" at its Madrid summit. A summit report said Romania and Slovenia were prime candidates for an expansion review in 1999.

Integration Minister Alexandru Herla told Wednesday's news conference that Romania was "better prepared for integration into NATO than the EU. The weak point for EU integration is our inability to implement community policies".
